title: A Fed official is asking whether AI is becoming ‘too big to fail’
excerpt: Kansas City Fed president Jeff Schmid says the sheer scale of AI investment now deserves scrutiny at a macro level, and raised whether the sector is becoming too big to fail.
content_html:
A senior Federal Reserve official has put an uncomfortable question on the table. Speaking this week, Kansas City Fed president Jeff Schmid said the finances around the AI buildout now merit close watching.

Jeff Schmid said there were signs the industry had grown large enough that policymakers should start discussing it at a macro level, and asked whether AI was becoming another sector that was too big to fail.

That phrase carries weight. It was the language of the 2008 financial crisis, when banks had grown so central that governments felt forced to rescue them, and hearing it applied to AI is a notable escalation in official tone.

Schmid’s worry is about scale and correlation. He suggested the current wave of AI spending should be compared with earlier booms, warning that concentration on this scale can turn a single sector’s troubles into an economy-wide problem.

The numbers behind the anxiety are staggering. Big Tech is now carrying nearly $2.4 trillion in AI spending commitments, a figure that dwarfs most previous corporate investment cycles and leaves little slack if demand disappoints.

It is not only the amount but how it is financed. The Bank for International Settlements has warned that an AI bust could hit credit markets as hard as 2008, precisely because so much of the buildout runs through debt and circular deals.

Those interlocking arrangements are what unsettle regulators. When chipmakers, cloud providers and model developers invest in one another, a stumble at any one node can ripple outward, and the exposure is harder to see from the outside.

Markets have started to notice. Nvidia’s wave of $750bn in AI deals pushed its credit default swaps to record levels, a sign that even lenders to the sector’s strongest name are pricing in more risk.

The comparison to past bubbles is not exact. On some measures the AI boom looks like the dot-com era, with valuations and concentration above 2000 levels, though the leading companies today are genuinely profitable in a way many 1999 darlings were not.

That is the knot facing the Fed. Real earnings make the boom look sturdier than a mania, yet the spending is so large and so leveraged that even a healthy sector could transmit shocks if sentiment turns.

Schmid’s comments also touch monetary policy. If AI investment keeps driving demand for power, chips and construction, it complicates the central bank’s reading of inflation and its decisions on interest rates.

The spending is also straining the companies themselves. Big Tech’s AI outlays are now catching up with its free cash flow, forcing firms that once funded everything internally to lean harder on debt and outside capital.

That shift is what pulls the Fed into the story. As financing moves from corporate balance sheets into credit markets and private lenders, the risk spreads to institutions the central bank is charged with watching.

Schmid is not alone in his unease. A growing chorus of officials and analysts has begun comparing the AI cycle to past manias, even as few are willing to call the top of a boom that keeps producing real revenue.

The practical worry is concentration. A handful of enormous firms now account for a large share of market gains and capital spending, so a stumble by any one of them would be felt far beyond the technology sector.

None of this amounts to a prediction of collapse. A Fed president musing about systemic risk is doing his job, and flagging a concern early is meant to prevent trouble rather than forecast it.

But the vocabulary matters. Once officials reach for the language of too big to fail, they are signalling that AI has moved from a market story to a question about the stability of the whole system.

content_html_zh:
一位美联储高级官员提出了一个令人不安的问题。 堪萨斯城联储主席杰夫施密德本周发表讲话表示，围绕人工智能建设的财务状况现在值得密切关注。

杰夫·施密德表示，有迹象表明该行业已经发展到足够大，政策制定者应该开始在宏观层面进行讨论，并询问人工智能是否正在成为另一个“大而不能倒”的行业。

这句话很有分量。 这是 2008 年金融危机时的用语，当时银行的地位如此之高，以至于政府感到被迫拯救它们，而听到它应用于人工智能，官方语气明显升级。

施密德的担忧在于规模和相关性。 他建议将当前的人工智能支出浪潮与之前的繁荣进行比较，并警告说，如此大规模的集中可能会将单个行业的问题变成整个经济的问题。

焦虑背后的数字是惊人的。 大型科技公司现在承担了近 2.4 万亿美元的人工智能支出承诺，这个数字使大多数以前的企业投资周期相形见绌，而且如果需求令人失望，也不会留有余地。

这不仅涉及金额，还涉及融资方式。 国际清算银行警告称，人工智能泡沫破灭对信贷市场的打击可能会像 2008 年一样严重，因为大部分的建设都是通过债务和循环交易进行的。

这些环环相扣的安排令监管机构感到不安。 当芯片制造商、云提供商和模型开发商相互投资时，任何一个节点的失误都可能向外蔓延，而从外部很难看到风险。

市场已经开始注意到这一点。 英伟达 7500 亿美元的人工智能交易浪潮将其信用违约互换推至创纪录水平，这表明即使是该行业最知名的贷款机构也在定价更多风险。

与过去泡沫的比较并不准确。 从某些指标来看，人工智能的繁荣看起来就像互联网时代，估值和集中度都在 2000 美元以上，尽管今天的领先公司确实实现了盈利，而许多 1999 年的宠儿却没有。

这是美联储面临的难题。 实际收益使繁荣看起来比狂热更强劲，但支出规模如此之大，杠杆如此之大，以至于如果情绪转变，即使是健康的行业也可能会传递冲击。

施密德的言论也触及货币政策。 如果人工智能投资继续推动电力、芯片和建筑的需求，那么央行对通胀的解读和利率决策就会变得复杂化。

这些支出也给公司本身带来了压力。 大型科技公司的人工智能支出现在正在赶上其自由现金流，迫使曾经为所有内部资金提供资金的公司更加依赖债务和外部资本。

这种转变正是美联储介入的原因。 随着融资从企业资产负债表转移到信贷市场和私人贷款机构，风险就会扩散到央行负责监管的机构。

施密德并不是唯一感到不安的人。 越来越多的官员和分析师开始将人工智能周期与过去的狂热进行比较，尽管很少有人愿意将持续产生实际收入的繁荣称为顶峰。

实际的担忧是注意力集中。 现在，少数几家大公司占据了市场收益和资本支出的很大一部分，因此，其中任何一家公司的失误都会远远超出科技行业的范围。

这些都不等于对崩溃的预测。 思考系统性风险的美联储主席正在尽自己的职责，尽早提出担忧是为了预防问题，而不是预测问题。

但词汇量很重要。 一旦官员们使用“太大而不能倒”的措辞，他们就表明人工智能已经从一个市场故事转变为一个关于整个系统稳定性的问题。
